title: Apologies, excuses and thanks
subtitle: I'm terribly sorry, I was held up, That's very kind of you
summary: Apologise in the right way for the situation, give an excuse, and thank people and reply to thanks.

lesson.heading: Saying sorry
lesson.text: To **apologise** means to say sorry. The words **terribly** and **really** make you sound 'more sorry'. **I beg your pardon** is a more formal apology, often used when you walk into someone.

examples.text: *A:* I'm (**terribly**/**really**) **sorry** - I've forgotten your book. *B:* Never mind. That's OK.
*A:* **I beg your pardon** - I didn't see you there. *B:* That's all right.

lesson.heading: Which apology in which situation
rows: you interrupt someone who is busy working
**I'm sorry to keep you waiting.** I won't be long.
someone is waiting for you; I won't be long = I'll be with you very soon
**Excuse me**, I won't be a minute.
you have to leave a room or go somewhere
**I must apologise for** the noise last night.
a more formal apology, often used in business letters
you arrive after the time you agreed
lesson.note: Common replies: Never mind. That's OK. That's all right. Don't worry. I understand.

lesson.text: Say **I'm sorry I'm late**, not ~~I'm sorry for be late~~ or ~~I'm sorry to be late~~.

lesson.heading: Excuses
lesson.text: After an apology we often give an explanation or **excuse** - a reason for the apology, which may or may not be true. These are excuses for being late.

examples.text: There was a **delay** on the underground.
examples.note: = a train or plane leaves or arrives later than you expect; you can also say a hold-up
hold up = cause a delay and make someone late; it is often used in the passive

examples.text: My train was **cancelled**, and I had to wait half an hour for the next one.
examples.note: = the train company decided not to run the train
= slept longer than I planned or wanted to

lesson.heading: Thanks and replies
lesson.text: **Thanks** and **cheers** are informal; **Thank you. That's very kind of you.** is polite and a little more formal. Common replies are **Not at all**, **That's OK** and **No problem**.

examples.text: *A:* I've brought your books. *B:* Oh, **cheers**. *A:* **No problem**.
examples.note: cheers and no problem are informal

examples.text: *A:* I'll post those letters for you. *B:* Oh, **thank you. That's very kind of you.**

left.label: Informal
left.text: With friends and people you know well.

right.label: More formal
right.text: With customers, in business letters, or with people you don't know.
examples: **Thank you. That's very kind of you.**

lesson.text: Learn apology and reply together: *I'm terribly sorry.* - *Never mind.* / *Sorry to keep you waiting.* - *That's all right.*

exercises.prompt: Match the phrases that have a similar meaning.

exercises.explanation: Not at all is a common reply to thanks.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Sorry to ___ you waiting. I won't be long. *B:* That's all right.
exercises.explanation: We say sorry to keep you waiting when someone is waiting for us.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Sorry to keep you waiting. I won't be ___.
exercises.hint: (one word - I'll be with you very soon)
exercises.explanation: I won't be long = I will be with you very soon.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I'm sorry I'm late. The 7:30 train was ___, so I had to wait for the next one.
exercises.hint: (the company decided not to run it)
exercises.explanation: If a train is cancelled, the company decides not to run it.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I gave your parents a lift to the station. *B:* Oh, thanks. That's very ___ of you.
exercises.explanation: That's very kind of you is a polite reply when someone helps you.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I must ___ for missing the meeting yesterday afternoon. *B:* Never mind.
exercises.explanation: I must apologise for ... is a more formal apology.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I ___ your pardon. I thought the room was empty. *B:* That's OK.
exercises.explanation: I beg your pardon is a formal apology, often used when you walk into someone.

exercises.prompt: You slept longer than you planned, so you say: 'I'm sorry I'm late - I ___.'
exercises.explanation: Oversleep = sleep longer than you planned or wanted to.

exercises.prompt: You need to speak to your boss, but she is working. What do you say when you enter her office?
options: I'm sorry to keep you waiting.
exercises.explanation: We say sorry to disturb you when we interrupt someone who is busy working.

exercises.prompt: You have to leave a meeting to take an important phone call. What do you say to the others?
options: Excuse me, I have to take an important phone call.
Never mind, I have to take a phone call.
Not at all, I have an important phone call.
Cheers, I have an important phone call.
exercises.explanation: We use Excuse me when we have to leave a room or go somewhere.

exercises.prompt: You are half an hour late because of the traffic. Give your excuse.
exercises.answer: I was held up in traffic.
exercises.explanation: Hold up means cause a delay, and it is usually used in the passive: I was held up.

exercises.statement: You arrive twenty minutes late and say: 'I'm sorry for be late.'
exercises.explanation: I'm sorry I'm late. We do not say ~~I'm sorry for be late~~.

exercises.statement: A man offers to help you push your broken-down car, so you say: 'Oh, thank you very much. That's very kind of you.'
exercises.explanation: Correct. That's very kind of you is the polite reply when someone offers help.
